Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be on guard all the time
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Triggers: Being Praised: Receiving praise or positive attention
issues.explanation: 'Being praised' is a hard-to-explain trigger in a profile otherwise centered on a life-threatening accident with sensory trigger cues, intrusive reliving, and hypervigilant threat monitoring. Unlike smell or darkness, praise has no evident link to the accident-based memory/threat pattern and stands out as clinically incoherent unless additional interpersonal trauma context were present.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Institutional failure' fits betrayal, assault, military, or disaster-response contexts more naturally than a single life-threatening accident in a financial analyst. In this profile the other appraisals focus on danger and inability to cope; this item introduces a qualitatively different blame/betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type, trigger pattern, or memory content.

vignette: Kai's eyes snapped open in the dead of night, his heart racing as he scanned the darkness for any sign of danger. It was a habit he'd developed since the accident six months ago, when his car had skidded off the road and crashed into a tree. He woke with a start, checking whether he was safe, only to find himself in his own bed, his wife sleeping peacefully beside him. As he lay there, Kai couldn't shake the feeling that his body reacted to danger before his mind did. It was as if his senses were constantly on high alert, ready to spring into action at a moment's notice. The slightest noise – the creak of the house settling, the sound of a car driving by outside – made him tense up, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios. Smells, too, had become a potent trigger for Kai. The scent of gasoline or burnt rubber would transport him back to that terrible night, and he'd be flooded with memories of the accident. He'd hear the sound of crunching metal, the shattering of glass, and his own voice screaming in terror. It was as if the memory was happening all over again, rather than being a distant recollection. Kai tried to avoid thinking about the accident, fearing that if he dwelled on it too long, he wouldn't be able to handle it. He'd become hypervigilant, constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats, and had developed a habit of checking for exits whenever he entered a room or building. It was exhausting, but he felt like he had no choice – after all, you never knew what could happen next. As the days turned into weeks, Kai found himself becoming increasingly withdrawn. He'd stopped going to his favorite coffee shop because it was too close to the intersection where the accident happened, and the smell of freshly brewed coffee would sometimes trigger a flashback. His work as a financial analyst had begun to suffer, too – he'd find himself zoning out in meetings, his mind preoccupied with worst-case scenarios. Kai's wife had tried to be supportive, but she didn't understand why he couldn't just "get over it." He felt like he was walking on eggshells all the time, never knowing when something would trigger a memory or send him into a panic. He'd become convinced that if he let his guard down for even a moment, disaster would strike. The cycle of fear and hypervigilance had become self-reinforcing, with each component feeding into the others. Kai's memories of the accident made him feel threatened, which in turn made him more vigilant, scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. And when he encountered triggers – smells, sounds, or dark spaces – it would all start again, a never-ending loop of fear and anxiety. It was this cycle that had finally brought Kai to seek help, as he realized that he couldn't keep living like this. He was tired of being controlled by his memories, tired of the constant sense of danger lurking just beneath the surface. With a deep breath, he reached out for support, hoping to break free from the grip of his PTSD and find some measure of peace.
